    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    It has been revealed that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    It has been revealed that picture this. A customer writes to your support chatbot: "Hi, I'm Asha, my card ending 4111 was charged twice, call me on 98400 12345." Your Java service wraps that message in a prompt, sends it to a model, and logs the whole thing so you can debug it later. Congratulations, you now have a customer's name, phone number and card details sitting in a plain text log file that half the engineering team can open.

    Recent findings suggest that this happens more often than people admit. Logging AI calls is genuinely useful, but prompts and responses are some of the most personal text your application ever touches. Here's how to keep the usefulness and drop the risk.

    Sources indicate that A regular web request is easy to log: URL, status code, time taken. AI calls are messier.

    The output changes from run to run. If a user says "your bot gave me a wrong answer yesterday", the only proof of what happened is what you sent and what came back at that moment. You can't just replay it and expect the same result.

    Prompts are also built, not typed. The final text is usually a template, a few retrieved document chunks, some chat history and the user's message stitched together. When something looks off, the bug could be in any of those pieces, and only the assembled prompt demonstrates you which one.

    Recent findings suggest that then there's cost. You pay by the token, so without per-call records you can't say which feature is burning money. And quality drifts over time as models get upgraded and templates get edited. Old logs are your only baseline.

    Recent findings suggest that so yes, you need these logs. The real question is what goes into them.

    Recent findings suggest that before writing any masking code, agree on what counts as sensitive. In most business apps that means:.

    Names, emails, phone numbers and home addresses.

    Card numbers, bank details and government ID numbers.

    Passwords, API keys and bearer tokens.

    Health, legal or job-related details people mention in free text.

    Internal material like contract wording, pricing rules or source code.

    According to recent reports, the first three groups follow patterns, so they're easy to catch. The last two don't, and that's where most teams get caught out. Keep that in mind, because it shapes the design below.

    The safest sensitive value is the one that never reaches the log. So split what you record into two buckets.

    In a recent development, the first is metadata: a request ID, a hashed user or tenant ID, model name, prompt template name and version, token counts, latency, retry count, error type and estimated cost. None of this is personal, and it answers most day-to-day questions.

    Industry observers note that the second is content, meaning the actual prompt and response text. You only need this when you're investigating quality, and even then you rarely need all of it. A sensible default is to log metadata for every call and masked content for a small sample, maybe five percent, plus every failed call.

    Here's a mistake that's easy to make: letting the log appender clean things up afterwards. By then the raw text may already be in a buffer, an async queue or a crash dump. Mask first, then log.

    The cleanest way is one small component that every AI log call has to pass through:.

    public interface PiiMasker {     String mask(String input); }.

    Industry observers note that nothing else is allowed to write raw prompts. One chokepoint is much easier to review and test than masking sprinkled across fifty classes.

    For structured data like emails, cards and tokens, regular expressions do the job well:.

    public class RegexPiiMasker implements PiiMasker {     private static final Map RULES = newly introduced LinkedHashMap<>();     static {         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9.%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}"), "[EMAIL]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("\b(?:\+?\d{1,3}[ -]?)?\d{10}\b"), "[PHONE]");         RULES.put(Pattern.compile("(?i)bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9.~+/=-]+"), "Bearer [TOKEN]");     }     @Override     public String mask(String input) {         if (input == null || input.isBlank()) return input;         String result = input;         for (var rule : RULES.entrySet()) {             result = rule.getKey().matcher(result).replaceAll(rule.getValue());         }         return result;     } }.

    A few small choices matter here. The patterns are compiled once, not on every call. The order is fixed, because a card number can otherwise get half eaten by the phone rule. And the replacement labels such as [EMAIL] keep the sentence readable, so whoever debugs it later can still follow what the user was asking.

    In a recent development, regex won't catch a name like "Asha Raman" or an address buried mid-sentence. For those you have a few options, and they work best together.

    In a recent development, you can run a named-entity recognition model that tags people, places and organisations, then mask anything above a confidence threshold. You can do exact replacement of values you already know, such as the customer's name from the current session. Or, best of all, you can mask at the field level while building the prompt. If your code knows that customer.getEmail() is going into the template, swap in a placeholder right there instead of trying to spot it afterwards. Knowing beats guessing every time.

    In a recent development, plain redaction can remove too much. If the same email shows up five times in a conversation, five identical [EMAIL] tags hide the fact that it was one person.

    According to recent reports, the fix is consistent pseudonyms. Turn each real value into a short token using a keyed hash, so the same email always becomes something like EMAIL_7f3a. You can still follow the thread, but nobody can read the original from the log. Use an HMAC with a secret from your secrets manager. A plain unkeyed hash of a phone number can be brute-forced in minutes, because there just aren't that many phone numbers.

    Recent findings suggest that one warning: if you also store a lookup table to reverse the tokens, that table is now sensitive data too. Most teams are better off with one-way tokens.

    Recent findings suggest that free-text log lines are hard to search and easy to leak through. Write one JSON record per AI call with clearly separate fields:.

    log.info("ai_call",     kv("requestId", requestId),     kv("model", model),     kv("promptVersion", "support-reply-v4"),     kv("inputTokens", usage.inputTokens()),     kv("outputTokens", usage.outputTokens()),     kv("latencyMs", elapsed),     kv("promptMasked", masker.mask(prompt)),     kv("responseMasked", masker.mask(response)));.

    Now dashboards for cost and latency never need to touch the text fields at all. You can also keep the two kinds of data for different lengths of time: metadata for a year, masked content for a couple of weeks. Put the request ID into your logging framework's MDC so every line belonging to one call, including retries and tool calls, carries the same ID.

    Recent findings suggest that streaming trips people up. Tokens arrive in tiny pieces, and a card number can be split across two chunks, which means masking each chunk on its own will miss it. Collect the full response in a buffer, mask it once the stream ends, and log that. If the stream dies halfway, run the partial buffer through the same masker.

    According to recent reports, tool calls are the other trap. When the model calls one of your Java methods, the arguments and return values are often the most sensitive thing in the whole exchange: order details, account balances, addresses. Treat them as part of the prompt and response. Log the tool name, duration and outcome by default, and log arguments only after masking.

    Masking lowers the risk but never removes it, so surround it with some ordinary discipline:.

    Give content fields a short retention period. Old prompt archives are liabilities.

    In a recent development, limit who can read AI logs. Debugging a model doesn't mean someone needs to read customer messages.

    Encrypt log storage and the pipeline that feeds it.

    Log the hashed user ID so you can find and delete one person's records when they ask.

    Allow verbose logging in development with fake data, and enforce strict settings in production through configuration, not through people remembering.

    It has been revealed that A masker that quietly stops working is worse than having none, because everyone assumes the logs are clean. Write tests for it:.

    @Test void masksEmailAndCardNumber() {     String raw = "Contact me at asha@example.com, card 4111 1111 1111 1111";     String safe = new RegexPiiMasker().mask(raw);     assertFalse(safe.contains("asha@example.com"));     assertFalse(safe.contains("4111"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[EMAIL]"));     assertTrue(safe.contains("[CARD]")); }.

    Sources indicate that build a small set of messy, realistic samples: numbers with odd spacing, mixed languages, addresses inside sentences, text pasted from spreadsheets. Run them in your CI pipeline, and add a new case every time a leak turns up. A scheduled job that scans stored logs for patterns that should never appear makes a good safety net too.

    Sources indicate that A few I'd watch for. Logging raw text at debug level and assuming production never enables it; debug flags get switched on during incidents, so mask at every level. Masking only the user's message while forgetting retrieved documents, system prompts and tool results. Letting SDK exceptions carry the full request body into the logs. Leaving wire-level HTTP logging on in production, which bypasses your masker completely. And treating masking as finished once it ships, when every latest prompt template can bring new kinds of data.

    Every AI call writes a structured metadata record with a request ID.

    All prompt and response text goes through a single masker first.

    Streams are masked after assembly, and tool arguments are masked too.

    Content logging is sampled, short-lived and access-controlled.

    Tests cover the masker, with a regression case for every past leak.

    Client libraries aren't dumping raw payloads into the logs.

    Recent findings suggest that good logs turn an AI feature from a black box into something you can actually debug, price and improve. The same logs can also expose the people who trusted you with their details. The way through is fairly plain: record metadata for every call, push all content through one well-tested masker, use pseudonyms when you need to follow a conversation, handle streams and tools carefully, and keep retention short. Set that up before launch, not after the first incident, and you get visibility without regret.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game.
    • It has been revealed that though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that apple has received much criticism for being late to the AI game. While OpenAI helped define the AI boom beginning in late 2021, and Google and other tech giants swiftly jumped on the AI train the following year, Apple didn’t make its first real foray into artificial intelligence until 2024 with Apple Intelligence. Though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings. In 2026, Apple made its AI system much more capable and expansive by introducing more advanced AI tools, including the Siri AI chatbot and Audio Intelligence. And just last month, Apple also debuted an additional AI tool dubbed “intelligent assistant.” The thing is, Apple now has so many AI offerings that it’s getting hard for the average consumer to keep track of what each one does, which devices support which AI tool, and which tools require a fee to access. So, here’s a cheat sheet for making sense of Apple’s increasingly confusing AI lineup. Apple Intelligence Apple Intelligence is the oldest of the tech giant’s modern AI offerings, introduced in 2024. Think of Apple Intelligence as the foundational artificial intelligence layer integrated into Apple’s operating systems, including iOS, macOS, and watchOS. Apple Intelligence includes a suite of smaller AI tools tailored to specific tasks. For example, Apple Intelligence powers Visual Intelligence, which lets Apple’s AI see and understand what’s on your screen or through your camera and take action on it; for example, it can tell you the nutritional information of the food on your plate. Apple Intelligence powers Audio Intelligence, a tool that can help you identify sounds and music and even recap your spoken conversations on some Apple Watches. It is also the engine behind numerous other AI features across your Apple products, including image generation, live translation, select photo editing tools, message summaries, and more. Not every device that supports Apple Intelligence supports all its features. Any Mac with an Apple Silicon chip will run Apple Intelligence, but you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12 GB of RAM or more to use some of its most advanced features, including custom Siri Voices and advanced AI dictation. For the iPhone, you’ll need an iPhone 17 Pro or later to use those advanced Apple Intelligence features (iPhone 15 Pro and later is required for most Apple Intelligence features). As for Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch, that’s limited to the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Series 4. Siri AI Siri AI is Apple’s new chatbot. Though people often use the terms “Siri AI” and “Apple Intelligence” interchangeably, they are actually distinct. Apple Intelligence is the foundational AI system integrated into Apple’s operating systems. Siri AI is the natural-language gateway to Apple Intelligence—it lets you communicate as you would with a person to give it commands or find information, which it then carries out using Apple Intelligence’s capabilities. Siri AI runs on the cloud on any device that supports iOS 27, macOS 27, iPadOS 27, visionOS 27, watchOS 27, and (soon) tvOS 27. However, if you want to run some aspects of Siri AI locally on your device, you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12GB of RAM or more, or an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, or later. Intelligent Assistant This is Apple’s newest major artificial intelligence tool, the most impressive, and the one that most muddies Apple’s AI branding. “Intelligent assistant,” introduced last month and released this month as part of the updated Logic Pro, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote apps in Apple’s paid Creator Studio suite, is a new natural-language AI tool aimed at helping creators be more productive. The tool is integrated into the above apps in the form of a chatbot. There’s a text field where you type instructions to the intelligent assistant (“make this piano track sound like it was recorded in a concert hall” or “fix the formula errors in this spreadsheet”). The changes happen like magic—all very impressive stuff. As a matter of fact, it’s way more impressive than the other capabilities Apple has shown off for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. So why hasn’t Apple branded these new AI features as Apple Intelligence? The answer: Intelligent assistant is not powered by Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. Instead, the new AI tools use Apple Foundation Models combined with additional models from third-party providers, in this case, OpenAI and Google. This explains why intelligent assistant is so capable (both OpenAI and Google have a huge lead over Apple in the AI space) and also why Apple has eschewed the Apple Intelligence branding for the work it carries out. Does Apple charge for AI? This is where things get really muddied for people. Apple’s AI pricing runs from free, to a monthly subscription fee, to higher usage limits with select iCloud Plus prepares. Presently, using Apple Intelligence and Siri AI is free for all consumers. However, Apple states this won’t last. With the release of the 27.3 versions of its operating systems in December, customers will have daily limits when using Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. If they exceed those limits, they won’t be able to use any Apple Intelligence features that require cloud processing (which costs Apple compute power). If users do want higher Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits, they can get more by paying for an iCloud Plus plan (if they don’t already have one). The 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which costs just 99 cents per month, doesn’t increase your AI limits. However, the other iCloud Plus plans do: 200GB ($2.99 per month): 2x limit increase 2TB ($9.99 per month): 5x limit increase 6TB ($29.99 per month): 10x limit increase 12TB ($59.99 per month): 20x limit increase As for intelligent assistant access in Logic Pro, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers, users already need to pony up. Intelligent assistant is available only as part of Apple’s Creator Studio subscription bundle, for which it charges $12.99 per month or $129 per year. This means that if you want as much access as possible to Apple’s AI offerings, you’ll need to subscribe to two subscription plans.

    Industry observers note that the thing is, Apple now has so many AI offerings that it’s getting hard for the average consumer to keep track of what each one does, which devices support which AI tool, and which tools require a fee to access. So, here’s a cheat sheet for making sense of Apple’s increasingly confusing AI lineup.

    Recent findings suggest that apple Intelligence is the oldest of the company’s modern AI offerings, introduced in 2024. Think of Apple Intelligence as the foundational artificial intelligence layer integrated into Apple’s operating systems, including iOS, macOS, and watchOS.

    According to recent reports, apple Intelligence includes a suite of smaller AI tools tailored to specific tasks. For example, Apple Intelligence powers Visual Intelligence, which lets Apple’s AI see and understand what’s on your screen or through your camera and take action on it; for example, it can tell you the nutritional information of the food on your plate.

    Apple Intelligence powers Audio Intelligence, a tool that can help you identify sounds and music and even recap your spoken conversations on some Apple Watches. It is also the engine behind numerous other AI features across your Apple products, including image generation, live translation, select photo editing tools, message summaries, and more.

    According to recent reports, not every device that supports Apple Intelligence supports all its features. Any Mac with an Apple Silicon chip will run Apple Intelligence, but you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12 GB of RAM or more to use some of its most advanced features, including custom Siri Voices and advanced AI dictation.

    For the iPhone, you’ll need an iPhone 17 Pro or later to use those advanced Apple Intelligence features (iPhone 15 Pro and later is required for most Apple Intelligence features). As for Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch, that’s limited to the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Series 4.

    Siri AI is Apple’s new chatbot. Though people often use the terms “Siri AI” and “Apple Intelligence” interchangeably, they are actually distinct.

    It has been revealed that apple Intelligence is the foundational AI system integrated into Apple’s operating systems. Siri AI is the natural-language gateway to Apple Intelligence—it lets you communicate as you would with a person to give it commands or find information, which it then carries out using Apple Intelligence’s capabilities.

    Recent findings suggest that siri AI runs on the cloud on any device that supports iOS 27, macOS 27, iPadOS 27, visionOS 27, watchOS 27, and (soon) tvOS 27. However, if you want to run some aspects of Siri AI locally on your device, you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12GB of RAM or more, or an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, or later.

    This is Apple’s newest major artificial intelligence tool, the most impressive, and the one that most muddies Apple’s AI branding.

    “Intelligent assistant,” introduced last month and released this month as part of the updated Logic Pro, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote apps in Apple’s paid Creator Studio suite, is a new natural-language AI tool aimed at helping creators be more productive.

    The tool is integrated into the above apps in the form of a chatbot. There’s a text field where you type instructions to the intelligent assistant (“make this piano track sound like it was recorded in a concert hall” or “fix the formula errors in this spreadsheet”). The changes happen like magic—all very impressive stuff.

    It has been revealed that as a matter of fact, it’s way more impressive than the other capabilities Apple has shown off for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. So why hasn’t Apple branded these new AI features as Apple Intelligence?

    Recent findings suggest that the answer: Intelligent assistant is not powered by Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. Instead, the new AI tools use Apple Foundation Models combined with additional models from third-party providers, in this case, OpenAI and Google. This explains why intelligent assistant is so capable (both OpenAI and Google have a huge lead over Apple in the AI space) and also why Apple has eschewed the Apple Intelligence branding for the work it carries out.

    This is where things get really muddied for people. Apple’s AI pricing runs from free, to a monthly subscription fee, to higher usage limits with select iCloud Plus plans.

    Recent findings suggest that currently, using Apple Intelligence and Siri AI is free for all customers. However, Apple states this won’t last. With the release of the 27.3 versions of its operating systems in December, customers will have daily limits when using Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. If they exceed those limits, they won’t be able to use any Apple Intelligence features that require cloud processing (which costs Apple compute power).

    If users do want higher Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits, they can get more by paying for an iCloud Plus blueprint (if they don’t already have one). The 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which costs just 99 cents per month, doesn’t increase your AI limits. However, the other iCloud Plus plans do:.

    According to recent reports, as for intelligent assistant access in Logic Pro, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers, people already need to pony up. Intelligent assistant is available only as part of Apple’s Creator Studio subscription bundle, for which it charges $12.99 per month or $129 per year.

    This means that if you want as much access as possible to Apple’s AI offerings, you’ll need to subscribe to two subscription plans.

    Hardware hacker builds open-source portable 3.5-inch floppy Wi-Fi NAS

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, hardware hacker BigCrimping (Crimp) has made a dedicated portable Wi-Fi NAS that allows for easily reading and copying 3.5" floppy disks over a network.
    • The upcoming device is called floppy3.5, and its design is completely open-source.
    • Sources indicate that the onboard monochrome LCD display looks pretty handy, as Crimp made it show a bevy of information, including sector and cylinder counts, a good/bad sector map, file counts, and even a firmware upgrade progress counter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, hardware hacker BigCrimping (Crimp) has made a dedicated portable Wi-Fi NAS that allows for easily reading and copying 3.5" floppy disks over a network. The renaissance of vintage hardware also extends to some early digital cameras, like the Sony Mavica and Panasonic PV-SD families. These point-and-shooters were popular due to using bog-standard 3.5" floppies in PC format. Many folks may still have floppies from this era around, or simply want to breathe upcoming life into their cameras.

    The upcoming device is called floppy3.5, and its design is completely open-source. Making one ought to be pretty easy, as Crimp made all the required files available on GitHub, including data for 3D printing the enclosure, and a custom PCB with an RP2354A microcontroller and an ESP32-S3 bridge. Besides those items, you'll need predictable necessities like a battery, a slimline floppy drive, a Wi-Fi module, and a microSD slot.

    Sources indicate that the onboard monochrome LCD display looks pretty handy, as Crimp made it show a bevy of information, including sector and cylinder counts, a good/bad sector map, file counts, and even a firmware upgrade progress counter. The onboard buttons do what they say: READ to scan the files, or SAVE to dump them to an SD card. The DISP and POWER buttons return you to the home screen, and power the device off and on.

    The card in said slot optionally stores the disk's files, allowing you to easily go around a storeroom or attic and just insert floppies one after another for archival without needing a computer. When it's time to manage content, you can access the floppy3.5's web interface over the network, and even connect to it directly with a USB cable if you need fancier features like fetching entire disk images.

    Crimp chose to use the Greaseweazle floppy drive comms protocol instead of relying on a conventional floppy drive controller. Besides saving on hardware, this allows full control over the drive, as Greaseweazle manages a drive's wire signals directly, making for easy imaging and all sorts of direct data manipulation, regardless of a disk's underlying format. By default, floppy3.5 understands FAT12 for its main purpose, but you can use the Greaseweazle utilities over the cable if needed.

    • Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter. Based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S. home prices rose 0.7% year over year from October 2025 to October 2026. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the 1.0% year-over-year increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the 1.3% year-over-year increase from August 2025 to August 2026. After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent run-up in long-term yields and mortgage rates. —> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window. —> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window. —> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window. We should point out that the nationally aggregated housing market is softer than the counts above suggest, given that year-over-year home price declines are right now skewed slightly toward larger metro areas. Home prices are still climbing a tad nominally (not inflation-adjusted) year over year in some pockets where active inventory remains well below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, such as certain areas in the Northeast and Midwest. In contrast, some pockets in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Colorado—where active inventory exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip—are seeing either material corrections, modest home price pullbacks, or simply flat pricing. Looking ahead, the significant question is how much of a burst of softening the nationally aggregated housing market will see, now that the 30-year fixed-mortgage rate has jumped back above 7.0% amid an already strained affordability environment and the still ongoing post-boom cyclical cooling period. To keep an eye on it, ResiClub recommends closely monitoring local active inventory/months of supply over the next several months. Click here for an interactive version of the chart below. Many of the housing markets seeing the most softness, where homebuyers have gained the most leverage since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, are primarily located in Sunbelt regions or the Mountain West. Many of these areas saw even greater price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home price growth outpacing local income levels. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose in 2022, markets like Tampa, Florida, and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices. That Sunbelt softening was further compounded by an abundance of latest-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives to maintain sales, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market. As a result, some buyers who might have previously opted for existing homes are instead choosing new construction with more attractive deals—which added further upward pressure to resale inventory growth over the past few years. Of course, while 76 of the nation’s 300 largest metro-area housing markets are seeing year-over-year home price declines, another 224 are seeing year-over-year home price increases. However, most of the places posting “nominal gains” are seeing gains below income growth and consumer price growth, which economists call “real” (inflation-adjusted) home price declines. Where are home prices still up on a year-over-year basis? See the map below. Below is a historical chart showing the year-over-year change in home prices across the 50 largest metro housing markets, with the yellow line representing the national aggregate, dating back to 2000. While the range [see chart above] between the strongest and weakest metro-area housing markets right now is fairly normal historically speaking, the bifurcation (i.e., direction) itself—the share of markets with rising home prices versus those with falling prices—is wider than normal, given that national appreciation is in a softer market with growth barely above 0.0%. And the longer some markets remain in the “rising” camp while others stay in the “falling” camp, the wider the gulf can become between the relatively more resilient markets and the weaker ones. For example, home prices in the Hartford, Conneticut, metro area are now 28.0% above their 2022 peak, while home prices in the Austin metro area sit 28.8% below their 2022 peak. Some of that bifurcation boils down to mean reversion, with many of the outright home price declines occurring in markets that overheated further during the pandemic housing boom. Note: For the historical chart below, we analyzed the 200 largest markets rather than the 300 used above, as some markets ranked 201 to 300 lack complete data going back to 2000. When weighted by population (not visualized), the housing market appears slightly weaker than the chart below suggests—which aligns with the fact that among just the 50 largest housing markets, 21 (42%) are currently posting negative year-over-year price growth, and nationally aggregated home prices are up just 0.7% year over year using the Zillow Home Value Index.

    Latest Update: Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.
    • I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy.
    • The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

    I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

    The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

    The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

    My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

    After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

    It has been revealed that despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

    If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

    In a recent development, tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

    It has been revealed that I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

    According to recent reports, we could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

    According to recent reports, I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the newly introduced connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

    This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

    In a recent development, when the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

    According to recent reports, swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That mentioned, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

    Sources indicate that I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”.

    With audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

    Recent findings suggest that this had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

    One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an revision, so here’s hoping.

    I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

    It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

    The experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

    Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

    Sources indicate that there is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

    #115756. Tech Report: Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

    Tech Report: Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
    • According to recent reports, over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
    • Industry observers note that the first button seems like pure theater to me.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the company announced two new switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics. The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help users avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just indicates less. [Image: Canva] Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like. Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off. The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company says its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics. [Image: Canva] Why, really The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library. These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company said in a statement. In an email, Canva says it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.” But if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your users and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The company says that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.” Perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva said that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The company also says it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company. Canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as quickly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”.

    #115755. One gigabyte of Wikipedia losslessly compressed to 105.39MB with self-learning AI transformer model

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (797 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

    One gigabyte of Wikipedia losslessly compressed to 105.39MB with self-learning AI transformer model

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (797 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tufa Labs’ tufazip has compressed 1GB of information from Wikipedia into just 105MB of space, losslessly, without using any hand-built models, according to a research post.
    • We shrank 1 GB of Wikipedia to 105.39 MB, losslessly.
    • According to recent reports, researcher Tommy He built tufazip, and the full package, at 105.39MB after optimization, includes a small, 4.33MB pre-trained starter model — stored at low precision, or quantized, to save space — that’s needed to unpack the file.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tufa Labs’ tufazip has compressed 1GB of information from Wikipedia into just 105MB of space, losslessly, without using any hand-built models, according to a research post. The method uses a 163-million-parameter Transformer model as a predictor instead, and similar compression or decompression would take two Nvidia B200 GPUs about a week to manage. It’s the smallest result on the Large Text Compression Benchmark from any entry that uses a neural network as its only predictor.

    We shrank 1 GB of Wikipedia to 105.39 MB, losslessly. Introducing tufazip: the best entry on the Large Text Compression Benchmark using a neural network as its sole predictor. Everything above it mixes a transformer with hand-built models.November 19, 2026.

    According to recent reports, researcher Tommy He built tufazip, and the full package, at 105.39MB after optimization, includes a small, 4.33MB pre-trained starter model — stored at low precision, or quantized, to save space — that’s needed to unpack the file. The full model is a 12-layer Transformer, which means there are 12 stages for each guess to go through. The starter stores just two already-trained stages, copying them back and forth to fill all 12 once the full model spins up in memory; each copy keeps learning on its own.

    This doesn’t work like a traditional chatbot or cloud AI but is, rather, a self-contained language model that learns on the fly. Notable here is that this compression is lossless, which means there’s no risk of any data being lost in the process. This means that predictor updates must be “fully deterministic.”.

    Training happens in two stages. The starter, a 34-million-parameter model, is trained offline, before any compression begins. Then, the full model begins to learn online, by predicting each token and training on it, with the unpacking side repeating the same steps, with the model itself being rebuilt alongside the text. For this reason, the total size must include, besides the compressed text, only the unpacking program and the files it needs, including the starter, but not the full trained model.

    Industry observers note that there is no traditional, hand-built compression model that assists, setting it apart, Tufa Labs notes, from all 12 entries that now rank above it on the benchmark, which mix a Transformer with hand-built models. Its first, online-only version ranked second when submitted in early September; the 105.39MB version was 13th as of the benchmark’s Nov. 19 enhancement. Emphasis should be placed on this being a text-only benchmark, for those imagining media files.

    While this sounds more exciting than, say, WinRAR, it’s for research purposes and not a product, and that’s underlined by what you’d need to actually run it. Presently, two Nvidia B200 GPUs — plus two Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPUs in the test machine — would need 631,548 seconds to compress and 645,748 seconds to decompress the 105.39MB version, or about 7.3 and 7.5 days, respectively, not counting the starter’s offline training.

    Sources indicate that the first version, which learned entirely online and came in at 105.98MB, took 647,595 and 630,136 seconds. Its GPUs peaked at 43.37 GiB of VRAM between them, and total memory use, GPUs included, peaked at roughly 68,525 MiB during compression and 73,748 MiB during decompression.

    Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

    7.3 days (excl. offline training).

    The experiment is fundamentally interesting because it demonstrates, for example, that a smaller vocabulary can actually help: a 4K-word tokenizer beats both 8K and 16K. Giving Wikipedia’s XML markup its own dedicated tokens made the compression worse. Bigger isn’t always better, and that goes for model size, too, as a 267-million-parameter model did slightly worse than a 188-million-parameter model on this data set. With a smaller, 100MB version of the file, gains leveled off at about 77 million parameters. A run started from a bigger, six-layer offline model predicted better, with just a 99.17MB payload, but its chunkier weights made the total file larger than the online-only run.

    Improving compression can be costly, as widening the window of already-processed text used for extra training, from 15 to 35 million tokens, only cut the payload 1.21% at the cost of 40% more compute. The key takeaways are that optimization isn’t always as simple as throwing more at the problem, and that trade-offs can be more expensive than expected. He frames that six-layer trade-off as the next research question: how much predictive quality a smaller model can keep, which makes the vanishing point a balance between predictive quality and model size for this benchmark.

    #115753. Players are coming to ‘GTA VI’ for the car chases, but staying for the wildlife

    📖 Baca

    Players are coming to ‘GTA VI’ for the car chases, but staying for the wildlife

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
    • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
    • The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal. The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map. Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date. GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person said that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life. Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players. “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.” In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise. Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.” Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the newly introduced installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture. One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023. In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the tech giant sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them. Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

    After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.

    The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.

    Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors.

    Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date.

    GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person remarked that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life.

    Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players.

    “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.”.

    In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise.

    Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, stated in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.”.

    Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.”.

    Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the newly introduced installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture.

    One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023.

    In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the tech giant sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them.

    Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

    Vivo X500 Pro camera review: Battle of the small(er) phones vs Pixel 11 Pro

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?
    • Over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company.
    • Industry observers note that the answer is mostly yes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The compact Vivo X500 Pro has some camera downgrades compared to the Pro Max, so are you better off saving money and getting the base Vivo X500 instead?

    Over the past few years, Vivo has made a name for itself as the camera powerhouse smartphone company. The first time I used a Vivo X100 Pro blew my mind in a way smartphone cameras hadn’t for a few years, but does the company’s 4th iteration — yes, Vivo skipped the X400 — of the X series still impress?

    Industry observers note that the answer is mostly yes. The Vivo X500 series includes five models: the base X500, the X500 Pro, and the X500 Pro Max. Unlike some other phones, all three of these models feature different camera hardware that takes advantage of the physical size differences. The X500 Pro Max’s hardware is the best of the bunch, but that phone is substantially larger and heavier as a result.

    So I’m comparing the more reasonably sized models to see which semi-compact Vivo phone you should consider this year. I tossed the Google Pixel 11 Pro into the comparison since Google also offers a compact flagship camera phone.

    Most camera specs between these phones are surprisingly comparable, so the differences you’re about to see are largely caused by some pretty massive differences in processing. I already covered Vivo’s wild new AI camera mode, so let’s go for something a little closer to normal smartphone camera use: a day at the Biltmore.

    Sources indicate that perhaps the biggest difference between these phones is Vivo’s pursuit of “perfection,” while Google seems to embrace a more “natural” look. At 10x and 5x, the photos from both Vivo phones are essentially noise-free, have clear sharpening applied to them, and are generally quite vibrant. Despite having similar specs, the Vivo X500 Pro’s more advanced Sony LYT telephoto sensor pulls out more detail.

    Google’s images are notably softer, although not in a low-resolution sort of way. They look more like they’re taken from a standard camera rather than a smartphone, which some people may prefer. While telephoto image quality between the Vivo X500 Pro and Google Pixel 11 Pro is mostly down to preference, Google’s phone is substantially faster while taking the actual photo. In all of the darker shots, the Pixel 11 Pro took the picture instantly. Both Vivo X500 models took a 2-3 second exposure shot, making me stand there for longer than I’m used to.

    Industry observers note that ultrawide performance is where I feel we see the largest gap between these phones. Both the Vivo X500 and X500 Pro cameras offer bright, well-balanced shots that are vibrant but not unrealistic. The light sources in the room emit a lovely warm glow, yet the bulbs themselves aren’t overblown. The X500 Pro’s slightly warmer image across all three scenarios looks best to me.

    The Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide images are often underexposed and lacking in dynamic range. The staircase shot exhibits this problem the most. This can come off as natural in some scenarios, as modern smartphone photography is notorious for brightening dark areas too much, but too often the Pixel 11 Pro’s ultrawide shots just feel unnaturally dark.

    The main camera is much more balanced, although it’s fun to push these phones to find their weaknesses. One of the best examples of differing priorities is in the wreath shot, which was quite dark in real life thanks to the bright sunlight outside. The Pixel 11 Pro valiantly tried to brighten up the shadows so you could actually see the wreath (since it’s clearly the subject), causing the rest of the scene to look forcefully bright.

    The same problem cropped up in the image of the wine rack, where both Vivo phones captured a nicer-looking shot. The image of the trellis walkway is a tie, but the photo of my ridiculous bowl of ice cream looks best on the Vivo X500 Pro, once again.

    Sources indicate that portrait mode is where I think the Vivo X500 Pro is the clear loser, but it’s not for any of the reasons in the other categories above. Rather, the X500 Pro seems to have some weird warping happening in the bokeh processing that’s not present on the base Vivo X500. This is in both front-facing and rear camera portrait shots, so it’s not a lens issue or some weird setting.

    Google cleaned up its portrait shots so much this year that it’s borderline ridiculous. Pixels had the worst portrait mode for years, but this year’s overhaul of the portrait algorithm made all the difference in the world.

    Overall, the Vivo X500 series is another solid release for Vivo, and while neither the base nor Pro models offer the same top-tier camera specs as the Pro Max model, it’s clear Vivo pulled off something great. The Vivo X500 Pro retails for €1,399 in the EU, while the base X500 global model is a little harder to find, but should be quite a bit cheaper if you can get your hands on it.

    #115749. Tech Report: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late
