    Tech Report: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5604 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
    • Industry observers note that some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed.
    • The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the organization.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in. Delegate Authority While Capacity Remains The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the firm. When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage. The turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the company’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank. Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated. Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited Archive Evidence Beyond External Platforms Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform. High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to. I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only demonstrates roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control. What I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a company or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ showed views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh. Your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it. Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC Ask for Help Before Depletion The decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them. I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It shows up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love. What I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a company. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet. Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group Broadcast Accomplishments to Gain Advocacy High performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret. I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their upcoming manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built. I’m now working with a younger employee with a new manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late. Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers Own Your Professional Future I’ve talked with more than a thousand executives in the past four years and the biggest regrets that I hear from high performers is relying on their employers to take care of them instead of taking ownership for their career decisions. I have had more clients than I can count who worked for Fortune 100 employers for 20+ years. They believed that they would retire with that company, but then the business changed, they lost their job, and they were left trying to figure out where to go next. No matter where you are in your career, you need to remember that companies are usually going to look out for themselves first. You need to plan your career accordingly. “Job hugging” has been the newest trend, where workers hang on to jobs that they don’t necessarily love. Sure, there is risk in leaving your job, but there is also risk at staying in your current job, especially if layoffs are on the horizon. Staying open to potential opportunities, both actively through networking and passively through an optimized LinkedIn profile, is key to building a career that lasts. Colleen Paulson, executive career consultant, Ageless Careers Align Ambition With Desired Work One decision high performers often make too late is to actively manage their careers rather than assuming that success in their current jobs will take care of that for them. Excelling at your job and managing your career are related, but they’re not the same thing. I’ve seen this play out in two ways. First, high performers become exceptionally good at identifying what it takes to succeed within their organizations. They earn promotions, navigate politics, and build expertise and relationships. But they don’t always stop to ask whether what they’re building is what they actually want. Over the last few years, I’ve worked with leaders who realized that the roles they’d spent years working toward had taken them further away from the work they loved, whether that’s working directly with clients or coaching their teams. We often think about the title and impact, but not the altitude we’ll have to lead at. A promotion often means moving away from doing the work yourself to creating the conditions for others to do it, through strategy, resource allocation, and management. That’s a very different job. Second, high performers forget to build career optionality before they need it. They invest heavily in building skills, relationships, and credibility within their organizations. That’s key, but incomplete. Internal recognition matters, but so does building an external professional network. Think of it as a savings account you’re contributing to over time. Too often, I’ve coached leaders who gave everything to their organizations, sometimes staying for more than a decade, only to find themselves facing a layoff, burnout, or a desire to pivot—and realizing they had limited external networks and little understanding of how their skills would translate elsewhere. A few simple ways to avoid these traps: • Before pursuing a promotion, talk to people already in the role. Understand what their day-to-day looks like, what they’ve had to give up, and what success actually requires. • While you’re happily employed, invest in relationships outside your organization and learn about other industries. Volunteer opportunities and nonprofit board service can be excellent ways to do this while also giving back. • The goal is not to constantly be on a job hunt. It’s to make sure you’re building a career that reflects what you want, with the flexibility to make different choices along the way. Lisa Friscia, president and founder, Franca Consulting Pursue Ventures Through Small Bets One decision high performers often regret making too late is waiting to act on an entrepreneurial idea because it feels safer to stay on secure footing. With more responsibility, high performers can get attached to income or get sucked into “golden handcuffs.” They’re less likely to leave for a more enjoyable job or take a risk at starting something up. I have seen this with seasoned corporate leaders who had a viable concept for years, but once they were settled with a mortgage, family responsibilities, and a stable role, the leap started to feel like too much to lose. The regret often sharpens when they later watch someone else succeed with a similar idea, because possibility suddenly looks like proof that they could have moved earlier. What could have been done differently is keeping the risk muscle active through small, regular bets while still employed, such as testing the idea in low-stakes ways and building comfort with uncertainty. That approach reduces the gap between the idea and bringing it to market, so the decision is not one big, intimidating jump. Also, it’s important to have accountability partners who ask us hard questions or challenge the status quo related to our experience, comfort, and career. How much money is enough? When is the right time? I hear high performers regret missed opportunities with a radical role departure or a job abroad or starting something new, going back to school when they were younger. We feel guilted or bullied into the norm by our families, peers, neighbors and society to do the “right” and “responsible” thing, then later wish we had taken the road less traveled or taken a risk. Janice Perkins, executive coach, Janice Perkins Restore Health Through Daily Habits The one decision high performers often regret is not focusing on their health and well-being as a function of improving their daily performance. All too often, high performers have had success all of their lives. They create habits in their 20s when their energy levels are high and their body can bounce back relatively quickly. As they start to advance their career in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, these high performers continue with these same habits, focusing only on work. Working late, missing sleep, skipping meals, and perhaps drinking alcohol (even in moderate amounts) drain more and more energy, physical and mental, from their daily output. To these habits, they add coffee to wake up and sugar intake to combat the energy crashes. This leads to poor sleep, and the cycle continues every day. It is possible to reverse these bad habits with small intentional changes in one’s daily lifestyle. A couple of simple examples are arising at the same time every day, including weekends, and getting morning daylight within the first 60-120 minutes of waking up. Steve Fiore, executive performance advisor, Rooted in Curiosity Serve Your Network Regularly As a career coach, I usually connect with high performers when they are in the midst of, or planning for, a transition. The #1 regret I hear is that leaders feel they lost touch with their network while building their careers. They understandably hesitate to make an ask when they haven’t connected in three, five, or even 10+ years. It can feel cringey and awkward reaching out when so much time has passed. But now more than ever, your network is your career net worth. So I hope more high achievers keep that in mind. The easiest way to keep in touch with your network? Be a helper. Haley McNeel Drake, résumé writer & career coach, The Career Revisory Exit Places That Diminish Your Worth One important decision I’ve seen time and time again among high performers is not leaving an organization sooner when their value went unrecognized. Being a high performer doesn’t automatically translate to timely promotions or special accolades for great work. In the pursuit of success, a high performer can work to increase their visibility and yet those efforts don’t lead to a promotion. Not because they’re doing anything wrong or focused on things that won’t get them noticed, but because of office politics or favoritism. What people often overlook and hate to admit is that you simply may be in the wrong environment where no matter what you do, your value will be unrecognized. For high performers, staying too long in an environment after making efforts to be “promotion ready” will eventually catch up, once they end up in an environment where they are valued, appreciated, and recognized for their work. Owning your competence, knowing your value, and being honest with yourself is part of high performance. Not getting a promotion the first time you ask for one isn’t necessarily a sign that you need to start looking or you’re being undervalued. However, the challenge arises when the same cycle repeats, and you’re getting empty promises instead of a kept word. Pay attention to nuance, yes: changes in the broader organization, natural attrition, etc. Timing is everything. But also, give yourself a timeline. If the opportunities you want to pursue don’t become available within that timeline, and those in charge can’t give you a blueprint to help you get where you want to be, you then make a different decision. And that could be planning your exit. Lisa De Nicola, leadership & executive coach; founder, HER Lead; Lisa De Nicola Broaden Expertise Outside Familiar Functions One decision high performers often make too late is stepping outside the area where they’ve already proven themselves. When you’re good at something, you tend to get more of it. You get promoted, take on bigger responsibilities, and become the person everyone relies on. That’s great for your career, but it can also keep you in a fairly narrow lane. Earlier in my career at HD Supply, I spent time working directly with branch managers, and one thing I did was lead financial literacy sessions. These were for people making decisions every day about pricing, inventory, customers, and how to run their businesses. I learned a tremendous amount from those conversations. They helped me understand the operating decisions behind the financial results, and that made me a much better finance leader. Looking back, I would have sought out more of that exposure earlier rather than waiting for opportunities to come through my formal responsibilities. My advice to high performers is to take on something outside your comfort zone before you feel completely ready. Spend time with customers, get involved in operations, or volunteer for a project that forces you to learn another part of the business. Being really good at your current job gets you noticed. Understanding how the whole business works prepares you for the next one. Thomas DeFabrizio, CFO, Vertage.

    Industry observers note that some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from protecting their health to asking for help and building stronger networks. These lessons offer clear steps for making better choices before regret sets in.

    The single decision high performers almost always make too late is firing themselves from day-to-day fulfillment, because their ego is still addicted to being the hero inside the organization.

    When I founded my first Scandinavian fine jewelry brand in Oslo at 22, I built our early momentum by personally touching every single bottleneck: approving every creative cut, negotiating every creator seeding deal, and rewriting campaign copy at 2:00 a.m. Because revenue was climbing and we were landing cultural placements like Khaby Lame and Vogue Scandinavia, I mistook exhaustion for leverage.

    According to recent reports, the turning point came when I realized that by being the best operator in the room, I had capped the organization’s valuation at the limit of my personal nervous system. High performers wait until they hit burnout to build standard operating procedures and delegate authority, whereas you actually have to hand off the keys while you still have 40% left in the tank.

    Once I forced myself to step out of daily order orchestration and document our visual and distribution protocols so the business ran without my fingerprints on every transaction, two things happened: Our enterprise value became transferable (allowing us to close a clean private acquisition exit in Q4 2024), and my own bandwidth opened up to direct film productions. If I could go back, I would have documented and delegated my favorite tasks 12 months earlier, not just the chores I hated.

    Mommi Live, founder, managing partner & creative director, Mommi Limited.

    Keeping their track record inside someone else’s platform.

    High performers usually build their reputation where the work happens: an employer’s system, a marketplace profile, a client’s internal tools. It feels like the record will always be there. Then the job ends, the platform changes its rules, or the old proof simply stops being shown, and years of results are hard to point to.

    It has been revealed that I learned this with my own business. I started selling video editing on Fiverr in 2020, while I was studying computer science. That grew into Mark Studios, which has completed more than 8,000 orders and earned 4,500+ reviews, with a 4.9 rating and Top Rated status. But Fiverr only reveals roughly the last two years of reviews, so the visible proof of the early years keeps shrinking even as the total grows. The work was real. The evidence just lived somewhere I didn’t control.

    Recent findings suggest that what I’d do differently, and what I tell anyone doing great work inside a company or a platform: Keep your own record from day one. Write a short case study after every project that matters, with the problem, what you did, and a measurable result. For a channel whose thumbnails and titles we’ve handled since August 2025, VidIQ showed views up 30.1% week over week when we captured the stats in May. That number now sits in a case study on my own website instead of only in a client conversation. Ask for testimonials you’re allowed to reuse, and save the numbers while they’re fresh.

    Recent findings suggest that your reputation is an asset. Make sure you hold a copy of it.

    Mark Santos, founder & creative director, Mark Studios LLC.

    The decision I see high performers regret most isn’t burning out. It’s waiting until they’re depleted to ask for help, because by then the choice is already gone. Their body makes it for them.

    Sources indicate that I’m a licensed counselor supervisor and president of a South Carolina practice with more than 60 therapists across 10 offices, plus online therapy. I watch this play out in my own field constantly. The strongest clinicians I supervise are usually the last ones to bring a hard case to supervision. Asking feels like admitting they can’t handle it, and they’ve built their whole identity around being the person others lean on. So they carry it quietly. And it doesn’t show up right away. It indicates up months later as irritability, or dread on Sunday nights, or a sudden wish to quit work they used to love.

    Sources indicate that what I tell them is pretty straightforward. Build the support in while things are still going well. Put a standing check-in on the calendar with a supervisor, a mentor, or a therapist before there’s anything urgent to report. When I started my practice with my husband, David, in 2019, I learned fast that the same logic applies to running a company. Support that you set up early costs you maybe an hour a week. Support that you set up late costs you a year of recovery. The best time to ask for help is when you don’t feel like you need it yet.

    Kenza Haddock, president, Oceanic Counseling Group.

    Industry observers note that high performers are great at getting things done, often to the detriment of their career progression. If you’re so busy taking care of things, then communicating out what you’re accomplishing is often the last thing on your list. That’s either because you don’t want to brag, or you assume others know what you’re working on. Not learning to communicate up and out is often a regret.

    I’ve worked with a senior leader whose manager was let go. They established relationships with their new manager and also with other senior leaders in the organization. They learned to communicate regularly as a part of their role to inform the what and the why of their accomplishments through one reorg after another. When yet another manager was let go, they were promoted into the role due to the awareness and extended support they’d built.

    According to recent reports, I’m now working with a younger employee with a newly introduced manager on how to own their weekly reporting, proactively communicating to the team what their weekly accomplishments are and how these fit into the greater goals. People can only advocate for you if they can say what you actually do. High performers often learn this alternate side of their role far too late.

    Dana Zellers, executive & leadership coach, team facilitator, Dana Zellers.

    I’ve talked with more than a thousand executives in the past four years and the biggest regrets that I hear from high performers is relying on their employers to take care of them instead of taking ownership for their career decisions.

    I have had more clients than I can count who worked for Fortune 100 employers for 20+ years. They believed that they would retire with that company, but then the business changed, they lost their job, and they were left trying to figure out where to go next.

    Recent findings suggest that no matter where you are in your career, you need to remember that companies are usually going to look out for themselves first. You need to blueprint your career accordingly. “Job hugging” has been the newest trend, where workers hang on to jobs that they don’t necessarily love. Sure, there is risk in leaving your job, but there is also risk at staying in your current job, especially if layoffs are on the horizon.

    Staying open to potential opportunities, both actively through networking and passively through an optimized LinkedIn profile, is key to building a career that lasts.

    Colleen Paulson, executive career consultant, Ageless Careers.

    Industry observers note that one decision high performers often make too late is to actively manage their careers rather than assuming that success in their current jobs will take care of that for them. Excelling at your job and managing your career are related, but they’re not the same thing. I’ve seen this play out in two ways.

    Recent findings suggest that first, high performers become exceptionally good at identifying what it takes to succeed within their organizations. They earn promotions, navigate politics, and build expertise and relationships. But they don’t always stop to ask whether what they’re building is what they actually want.

    According to recent reports, over the last few years, I’ve worked with leaders who realized that the roles they’d spent years working toward had taken them further away from the work they loved, whether that’s working directly with clients or coaching their teams. We often think about the title and impact, but not the altitude we’ll have to lead at. A promotion often means moving away from doing the work yourself to creating the conditions for others to do it, through strategy, resource allocation, and management. That’s a very different job.

    Second, high performers forget to build career optionality before they need it. They invest heavily in building skills, relationships, and credibility within their organizations. That’s important, but incomplete. Internal recognition matters, but so does building an external professional network. Think of it as a savings account you’re contributing to over time.

    Too often, I’ve coached leaders who gave everything to their organizations, sometimes staying for more than a decade, only to find themselves facing a layoff, burnout, or a desire to pivot—and realizing they had limited external networks and little understanding of how their skills would translate elsewhere.

    A few simple ways to avoid these traps:.

    In a recent development, • Before pursuing a promotion, talk to people already in the role. Understand what their day-to-day looks like, what they’ve had to give up, and what success actually requires.

    • While you’re happily employed, invest in relationships outside your organization and learn about other industries. Volunteer opportunities and nonprofit board service can be excellent ways to do this while also giving back.

    • The goal is not to constantly be on a job hunt. It’s to make sure you’re building a career that reflects what you want, with the flexibility to make different choices along the way.

    Lisa Friscia, president and founder, Franca Consulting.

    One decision high performers often regret making too late is waiting to act on an entrepreneurial idea because it feels safer to stay on secure footing. With more responsibility, high performers can get attached to income or get sucked into “golden handcuffs.” They’re less likely to leave for a more enjoyable job or take a risk at starting something up. I have seen this with seasoned corporate leaders who had a viable concept for years, but once they were settled with a mortgage, family responsibilities, and a stable role, the leap started to feel like too much to lose.

    The regret often sharpens when they later watch someone else succeed with a similar idea, because possibility suddenly looks like proof that they could have moved earlier. What could have been done differently is keeping the risk muscle active through small, regular bets while still employed, such as testing the idea in low-stakes ways and building comfort with uncertainty. That approach reduces the gap between the idea and bringing it to market, so the decision is not one massive, intimidating jump.

    Sources indicate that also, it’s important to have accountability partners who ask us hard questions or challenge the status quo related to our experience, comfort, and career. How much money is enough? When is the right time? I hear high performers regret missed opportunities with a radical role departure or a job abroad or starting something newly introduced, going back to school when they were younger. We feel guilted or bullied into the norm by our families, peers, neighbors and society to do the “right” and “responsible” thing, then later wish we had taken the road less traveled or taken a risk.

    Janice Perkins, executive coach, Janice Perkins.

    The one decision high performers often regret is not focusing on their health and well-being as a function of improving their daily performance.

    All too often, high performers have had success all of their lives. They create habits in their 20s when their energy levels are high and their body can bounce back relatively swiftly. As they start to advance their career in their 30s, 40s, and 50s, these high performers continue with these same habits, focusing only on work. Working late, missing sleep, skipping meals, and perhaps drinking alcohol (even in moderate amounts) drain more and more energy, physical and mental, from their daily output.

    Sources indicate that to these habits, they add coffee to wake up and sugar intake to combat the energy crashes. This leads to poor sleep, and the cycle continues every day.

    Industry observers note that it is possible to reverse these bad habits with small intentional changes in one’s daily lifestyle. A couple of simple examples are arising at the same time every day, including weekends, and getting morning daylight within the first 60-120 minutes of waking up.

    Steve Fiore, executive performance advisor, Rooted in Curiosity.

    It has been revealed that as a career coach, I usually connect with high performers when they are in the midst of, or planning for, a transition. The #1 regret I hear is that leaders feel they lost touch with their network while building their careers.

    It has been revealed that they understandably hesitate to make an ask when they haven’t connected in three, five, or even 10+ years. It can feel cringey and awkward reaching out when so much time has passed.

    Industry observers note that but now more than ever, your network is your career net worth. So I hope more high achievers keep that in mind.

    Sources indicate that the easiest way to keep in touch with your network? Be a helper.

    Haley McNeel Drake, résumé writer & career coach, The Career Revisory.

    One crucial decision I’ve seen time and time again among high performers is not leaving an organization sooner when their value went unrecognized. Being a high performer doesn’t automatically translate to timely promotions or special accolades for great work.

    Industry observers note that in the pursuit of success, a high performer can work to increase their visibility and yet those efforts don’t lead to a promotion. Not because they’re doing anything wrong or focused on things that won’t get them noticed, but because of office politics or favoritism. What people often overlook and hate to admit is that you simply may be in the wrong environment where no matter what you do, your value will be unrecognized.

    For high performers, staying too long in an environment after making efforts to be “promotion ready” will eventually catch up, once they end up in an environment where they are valued, appreciated, and recognized for their work.

    Owning your competence, knowing your value, and being honest with yourself is part of high performance. Not getting a promotion the first time you ask for one isn’t necessarily a sign that you need to start looking or you’re being undervalued. However, the challenge arises when the same cycle repeats, and you’re getting empty promises instead of a kept word.

    According to recent reports, pay attention to nuance, yes: changes in the broader organization, natural attrition, etc. Timing is everything. But also, give yourself a timeline. If the opportunities you want to pursue don’t become available within that timeline, and those in charge can’t give you a blueprint to help you get where you want to be, you then make a different decision. And that could be planning your exit.

    Lisa De Nicola, leadership & executive coach; founder, HER Lead; Lisa De Nicola.

    One decision high performers often make too late is stepping outside the area where they’ve already proven themselves.

    According to recent reports, when you’re good at something, you tend to get more of it. You get promoted, take on bigger responsibilities, and become the person everyone relies on. That’s great for your career, but it can also keep you in a fairly narrow lane.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier in my career at HD Supply, I spent time working directly with branch managers, and one thing I did was lead financial literacy sessions. These were for people making decisions every day about pricing, inventory, customers, and how to run their businesses.

    I learned a tremendous amount from those conversations. They helped me understand the operating decisions behind the financial results, and that made me a much better finance leader.

    Looking back, I would have sought out more of that exposure earlier rather than waiting for opportunities to come through my formal responsibilities.

    My advice to high performers is to take on something outside your comfort zone before you feel completely ready. Spend time with customers, get involved in operations, or volunteer for a project that forces you to learn another part of the business.

    Being really good at your current job gets you noticed. Understanding how the whole business works prepares you for the next one.

    Thomas DeFabrizio, CFO, Vertage.

    A visitor clicks a search ad, submits a quote request, and calls your sales team ten minutes later. The form integration creates a CRM contact. The phone platform records a call. By Friday, the marketing report demonstrates two leads, while sales remembers one conversation that turned into a deal.

    Industry observers note that both systems captured something useful. The problem is that neither record explains how the two interactions belong together.

    A unified tracking pipeline gives forms and calls a common event format, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to CRM outcomes. It also needs to survive a less tidy reality: repeated callbacks, missing campaign data, delayed updates, and a CRM that occasionally refuses requests.

    In a recent development, this tutorial builds the core of that pipeline with JavaScript and PostgreSQL. We will capture campaign parameters, define a shared event contract, and persist events alongside the work needed to deliver them. Provider authentication and CRM requests belong in adapters around this core, using the documentation for the services you choose.

    According to recent reports, before writing an endpoint, decide what you are counting. A phone call can produce several status callbacks. A person can submit two forms. An existing customer can contact sales about a new purchase.

    Use separate identifiers for these different things:.

    This separation prevents two common mistakes. Deduplicating by call ID alone can discard later status updates. Counting every callback as a lead inflates demand.

    According to recent reports, for this implementation, each event is unique within a tenant and source. A tenant is the business whose data you are processing; the source identifies a website or provider account. The same provider event ID can therefore appear in two accounts without causing a collision.

    Keep the original interactions even after you connect them to one contact. The form and the call are both useful evidence. Your reporting layer decides whether they represent one opportunity.

    Campaign parameters are easiest to capture when the visitor first arrives. Waiting until the form submission can lose them if the visitor has already moved to another page.

    According to recent reports, google's campaign URL documentation explains the roles of utm_source, utm_medium, and utm_campaign. The following helper reads those fields and a few optional ones, without copying the entire query string:.

    In a recent development, the browser's URLSearchParams interface handles query parsing and decoding. It saves you from writing string-splitting code that breaks on encoded characters.

    Run this helper through your site's existing consent and attribution flow. Where storage is permitted, associate the result with an opaque attribution reference in your backend and retain that reference through the visit. A later form submission sends the reference; the server resolves it within the correct tenant and visitor session. The form must still work when attribution storage is unavailable.

    Keep first-touch and current-touch records separately if you need both. Overwriting the first campaign every time someone returns makes the eventual report answer a different question.

    According to recent reports, treat campaign labels as untrusted input. Visitors can edit query strings and hidden fields. Validate them on the server, escape them when displayed, and never use them as authorization or as the sole evidence for commission payments. Avoid putting names, email addresses, or other personal information in UTM values.

    Recent findings suggest that missing tags also need careful handling. An empty UTM object only tells you that no accepted UTM values were captured. Classifying a visit as direct, organic, or referral requires additional evidence and an explicit attribution rule.

    Forms carry browser context naturally. Phone calls need a bridge between the number dialed and the marketing interaction that prompted the call.

    Sources indicate that there are two useful levels of precision. A number assigned to one campaign can identify that campaign. Dynamic number insertion can support a more detailed association by displaying tracking numbers according to a visitor or session mapping. That association depends on the provider's number allocation and expiry rules.

    Sources indicate that providers differ in how they implement this, and in what they expose beyond it, such as keyword-level reporting or conversation analysis. If you are still choosing one, this comparison of attribution software with call tracking is a useful starting point. At the integration boundary, check which event identifiers, attribution fields, delivery mechanisms, and authentication options your configured product exposes.

    Industry observers note that keep that provider-specific work in an adapter. Its job is to turn an authenticated notification into your event contract and resolve any attribution reference supported by the provider's data. The application schema below is an internal contract; each provider adapter translates its documented payload into that contract.

    Store the basis of a match with the attribution record. For example, session_match, campaign_number, and unknown make different levels of evidence visible to reporting. If a number has been reassigned, use the mapping valid when the call occurred, not whichever mapping happens to be current when the callback arrives. If the evidence is ambiguous, leave the association unresolved.

    Sources indicate that caller ID is a separate matter. A shared office number, a withheld number, or an outdated contact record can make automatic identity matching unreliable. A confirmed CRM contact ID or an authenticated account provides a stronger link. Treat a matching phone number as a candidate for reconciliation rather than proof that two records belong to the same person.

    It has been revealed that A shared event envelope lets the rest of your application work with a small, predictable vocabulary. Here is an illustrative call event:.

    "occurred_at": "2026-11-06T10:14:00.000Z",.

    "data": { "status": "completed" }.

    The event ID identifies this occurrence. The interaction ID groups it with other events for the same call. contact_ref can remain empty until you have enough evidence to connect the interaction to a contact.

    Keep contact details in a controlled contact store and campaign details in an attribution store. The references above point to those records; they are not credentials and must not grant access on their own.

    It has been revealed that the following factory checks the shared envelope. Each adapter still needs its own validation for provider fields and the contents of data.

    Resolve trusted from server configuration and the authenticated integration. Never let a submitted tenant_id choose whose records a webhook can write. Resolve contact and attribution references within that same tenant.

    According to recent reports, for a form, problem a submission ID and reuse it when retrying the same submission. Generate a fresh one when the visitor deliberately starts another inquiry. Preserve the originally accepted timestamp as well. For a phone event, prefer the provider's stable event ID. If the provider documents a sequence number, a call ID plus that sequence can identify an occurrence within a provider account.

    Twilio's call resource documentation provides a concrete example: call progress callbacks include a SequenceNumber, and separate HTTP requests can arrive out of order. Preserve that sequence in the adapter. A late “ringing” event should remain in the history without replacing a newer terminal state.

    Industry observers note that authenticate before calling this factory. Use the provider's supported validator and the exact request representation it requires. Twilio's webhook security guide describes signature validation, including the importance of the request URL and payload. Other providers may use different mechanisms. Public form endpoints need their own input limits, abuse controls, and appropriate CSRF protection.

    Industry observers note that consider a failure between these two operations: the application saves an event, then crashes before scheduling its CRM update. The event exists, but nothing is waiting to deliver it.

    A transactional outbox addresses that gap. Save the event and a delivery task in the same database transaction, then let a worker process the task. AWS explains this dual-write problem in its transactional outbox guidance.

    Here is a compact schema. received_at records ingestion time, while the envelope retains the event's original occurred_at value.

    available_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),.

    attempts integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,.

    UNIQUE (tenant_id, source, event_id),.

    FOREIGN KEY (tenant_id, source, event_id).

    REFERENCES lead_events (tenant_id, source, event_id).

    It has been revealed that postgreSQL's INSERT documentation defines the conflict handling used here. The unique key makes duplicate detection hold across application processes. A duplicate with the same normalized payload creates no second task; reuse of the key with different data raises a conflict for investigation.

    Sources indicate that this depends on immutable event bodies. Do not add a fresh receipt timestamp, random identifier, or current CRM status to the normalized payload on each delivery. Store later enrichment separately or emit a latest event. Otherwise an ordinary retry will appear to be a conflicting event.

    The function deliberately uses one database client throughout the transaction, as required by the node-postgres transaction documentation. Parameter values are passed separately from SQL, following its parameterized query guidance.

    After this function commits, acknowledge the notification using the response expected by the sender. An identical duplicate should also receive a successful acknowledgement. If persistence fails, return the appropriate failure response and rely on the configured retry or reconciliation process. A success response sent before durable storage can turn a temporary database failure into a missing event.

    In a recent development, for voice integrations, distinguish an informational status callback from a request asking your application how to handle a live call. They can require different response bodies, as explained in the Twilio webhooks FAQ.

    The outbox gives you durable work to process. It does not make a remote CRM operation happen exactly once.

    Sources indicate that imagine the CRM saves an update, but the worker crashes before setting processed_at. When the task runs again, the same request may reach the CRM twice. Design for that case explicitly.

    According to recent reports, use a stable external identifier for each contact, opportunity, and activity, and check which deduplication guarantees the destination supports. HubSpot's contacts API documentation, for example, describes upserts using unique properties. Support for a contact upsert does not automatically make every associated activity or workflow idempotent. Verify the behavior of each operation you send.

    In a recent development, if the destination cannot deduplicate a create request and a timeout leaves its result uncertain, reconcile that operation before repeating it. A local “sent” flag alone cannot prove whether the remote write happened.

    The worker should claim due tasks, commit a recoverable lease, and perform network calls outside the database transaction. A lease allows another worker to recover work after a crash. When multiple workers poll the outbox, PostgreSQL's SKIP LOCKED behavior can help claim separate rows, but the lease and its recovery logic still need to be implemented.

    Sources indicate that retry transient failures with increasing delays and jitter. Respect the destination's rate-limit instructions. Send persistent validation failures to a review queue with a useful error category, and provide a way to replay them after correction. The schema above is the ingestion foundation; a production worker needs lease fields, failure details, and a retry policy appropriate to its destination.

    According to recent reports, also preserve ordering where it changes meaning. If two events update the same contact or opportunity, process them serially or reject stale updates using a stored version. A historical event should not move a won opportunity back to an earlier stage.

    It has been revealed that once both channels reach the CRM, connect them to the result the business cares about. A form submission is an inquiry. A completed phone call is a technical outcome. Neither alone establishes that a lead qualified or a purchase happened. If agents record call dispositions, such as whether a call was qualified or transferred to a closer, that field is a richer signal than call completion status alone.

    Sources indicate that have the CRM or the system that owns the transaction emit explicit outcome events, such as lead.qualified and deal.won. Include the internal opportunity ID and the original outcome time. Model reversals or cancellations explicitly if they affect revenue reporting.

    Then choose the unit behind each metric. For a report about opportunities acquired during a particular month, a qualification rate can use qualified opportunities divided by all opportunities in that acquisition cohort. Counting qualification events received during the month would answer a different question and could include older inquiries.

    Deduplicate opportunities before calculating channel totals. A person who submits a form and calls about the same purchase should retain both interactions, while the opportunity receives credit according to your chosen attribution rule. Label that rule in the report so first-touch and last-touch numbers are not compared as though they measure the same thing.

    Measure data quality alongside performance. Track unresolved attribution, duplicate deliveries, ingestion failures, and the age of the oldest pending outbox task. Once several sources and destinations feed the same reports, a data observability platform can watch these signals across the whole pipeline instead of relying on checks inside a single worker. An apparently quiet campaign may actually have a broken integration.

    Operational logs should contain enough context to investigate failures without becoming another customer database. Use internal references and error categories, and avoid dumping webhook bodies into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet provides guidance on excluding or protecting sensitive values.

    A successful form submission proves little about retries or missing data. Before connecting production traffic, test the cases that could distort reporting or lose an inquiry.

    Sources indicate that run database cases against PostgreSQL with separate connections so the tests exercise actual constraints and transaction behavior. Use the provider's test tools or signed fixtures for webhook authentication. Test CRM retries against a sandbox with the destination's real duplicate-handling rules.

    Start rollout with one form and one phone source. Trace a known inquiry from its captured campaign through its interactions to its CRM outcome. Reconcile event totals against the source systems over the same time window, allowing for delivery delays. Expand once that path is explainable and failures are visible.

    Industry observers note that the same adapter pattern extends to inquiries that start offline, such as leads collected at a trade show and exported as a CSV or XLSX file. Import each row as a form.submitted event with the event as its source, a stable row identifier as event_id, and the original capture time as occurred_at. Because the outbox treats an identical event as a duplicate, re-importing the same export won’t create a second CRM task.

    What is a unified lead tracking pipeline?

    In a recent development, it is a workflow that converts inquiries from different channels into a shared data model, preserves their acquisition context, and connects them to business outcomes. Forms and calls keep their own interaction records, while contacts and opportunities provide the relationships needed for reporting.

    Can I connect a phone call to a website visit?

    Sometimes. Dynamic number insertion can provide a session or visitor association when the provider's mapping is available and valid. A campaign-specific number usually supports campaign-level attribution. If the caller uses a saved number, switches devices, or calls after a mapping expires, the available evidence may be less precise.

    How do I prevent duplicate leads?

    Sources indicate that handle duplicate delivery and identity resolution separately. Stable event IDs and a database constraint prevent repeated notifications from producing repeated work. Connecting several interactions to one contact or opportunity requires a separate matching policy, with ambiguous cases left unresolved until there is enough evidence.

    Should a completed call count as a conversion?

    Sources indicate that only if that is the conversion your report explicitly measures. A completed call does not establish that a prospect qualified or bought something. Keep technical call status separate from CRM outcomes and use the latter when reporting qualified demand or revenue.

    Do I need a message broker for this architecture?

    Industry observers note that you can begin with PostgreSQL and an outbox worker if that setup meets your throughput and latency needs. A broker becomes useful when several consumers need independent delivery, or when buffering and scale justify the additional operations. In either case, retries still require idempotent consumers.

    What happens when tracking consent is unavailable?

    Keep the inquiry flow usable and apply your site's existing consent rules to optional attribution collection and storage. Accept permitted form or call data, leave unavailable attribution empty, and avoid reconstructing a visitor identity through fingerprinting. Reports should expose that missing context instead of inventing a campaign match.

    Google Play wants Android apps to nail foldable basics by April 2027

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (336 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Play is introducing latest adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.
    • Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.
    • Referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Play is introducing latest adaptive app and game quality requirements next year to elevate the Android foldable experience.

    Starting April 2027, the Play Store will require developers to meet Tier 3 of the Android adaptive app quality guidelines for foldables.

    Referred to as “Adaptive ready” or “basic” support, Tier 3 requires apps not to use letterboxing (or other compatibility modes) and to fill the entire screen. During rotation, resizing, and folding/unfolding, apps must preserve scroll position, text input, and media playback. Apps must also support multi-window environments.

    Apps that do not meet this quality bar will no longer be able to publish or upgrade on Google Play, and may have reduced visibility on the store.

    At the same time, Google Play will require foldable device screenshots for app listings: “Providing foldable screenshots by April 2027 will become a standard submission requirement when publishing new apps or updating your store listing.”.

    Curious to see whether the requirements will actually be as strict as they make them seem (on paper).

    If so, then also Google will have a ton of work to do to modernise all of their apps.

    By August 2027, new and updated apps will be required to target Android 17 (API level 37).

    Over time, this “quality framework will progressively expand to incorporate Tier 2 and Tier 1 standards across foldables, tablets, Googlebooks, and Android XR.”.

    Apps that meet Tier 2 (better) or Tier 1 (best) will get “premier store badging, editorial spotlighting, and enhanced merchandising across Google Play as the platform bar elevates.”.

    On the gaming front, titles will need to add foldable screenshots to listings by April 2027, while Tier 3 large screen quality guidelines go into effect in August 2027.

    #115746. To win the AI search wars, stop chasing the answers and start shaping the questions

    To win the AI search wars, stop chasing the answers and start shaping the questions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1522 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that AI is changing how people choose between brands.
    • In a recent development, AI is changing how people choose between brands.
    • Personal agents like Meta’s Muse take their cues from things like your email inbox and run with what they find.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that AI is changing how people choose between brands. And it’s moving from answering people’s questions to taking action on their behalf. Personal agents like Meta’s Muse take their cues from things like your email inbox and run with what they find. Now if that sounds scary, you’re behind the curve. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada started using Muse in its first six weeks. The number one thing they’re using it for? Shopping. And not just for massive purchases. In a McKinsey survey across 11 markets, nearly one-third (29%) of people who shop with artificial intelligence noted it was the strongest influence on their last purchase. Groceries are now the second most common thing people buy directly inside an AI tool, just behind clothes. Availability bias Historically, brands have grown on the back of a human shortcut called availability bias. When it comes to most everyday choices, the average person instinctively reaches for the brand that’s first to mind and first to find. AI behaves differently. It’s more literal than it is lazy, and the same is true whether it’s ChatGPT or a Grok Bot. It favors well-known brands when everything else is equal. In a recent study of AI skincare recommendations, the models picked the well-known brand every time when the products were identical. But give a lesser-known rival a rating that’s even less than a tenth of a star higher, and that stopped. Most of the time AI is prepared to compare, matching what a person wants against what a brand delivers. No wonder then that generative engine optimization (GEO), which means making sure your brand is the answer when someone asks AI, has become big business. And it works. BCG reports that a luxury fashion group fixed the structured data behind its website, and within eight weeks the rate at which AI search linked to its site had more than doubled. The problem is that it mostly works when you’re the only one doing it. In the skincare study, when every brand used the same technique, the gains all but canceled out, and brands that sat it out disappeared from the recommendations. GEO looks destined to become a cost of entry, not an advantage. A better way So, is there a better way? Rather than chasing the answer, what if a brand could shape the question people ask? Every choice has two sides: the person’s criteria and the brand’s attributes. A brand gets chosen when the two line up. GEO is about optimizing how a brand presents its attributes. What I’m suggesting is optimizing the criteria people bring. Marketing has a track record of changing what’s key to people. Brands can make things matter more than they’ve mattered before. Volvo, for example, made safety the way to judge a car. Nike did the same for cushioning in running shoes. Others changed how people judge. Dyson moved vacuums from suction power to suction that lasts. Avis moved car rentals from who’s biggest to who tries hardest. And some gave people something new to look for, as Head & Shoulders did with dandruff. Better still, frame the question around an attribute only you have. Ask AI for the best phone for FaceTime and there’s only one answer, and 88% of American teenagers already own an iPhone, according to a spring 2025 survey from Piper Sandler, the investment bank. In China, where people choose skincare by ingredient, L’Oréal’s Pro-Xylane became one of the most sought after, and only L’Oréal brands can use the name. Where do you start? Find the attribute you win on, relative to your size, and check that people and AI agree. If they disagree, shaping the question can backfire. If people believe something about your brand and AI doesn’t, you make the question matter and AI recommends a rival. If AI believes something about your brand and people don’t, AI recommends you, but nobody asks. Consider Dr. Whitney Bowe, the New York dermatologist who coined “skin cycling” on TikTok. She gave people a new question to ask, and retailers like Boots published guides on what to buy for it. Then she launched her own brand, with a skin-cycling kit. She shaped the question, then built the brand to answer it. Maybe there are two new questions for every brief from here on out. What attribute do we win on? What question do we want people to ask? Shape the question, and you won’t have to chase the answer.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that microsoft systems down. Air traffic systems down. Problems at Chase, United, and Apple. After a week of outages across big systems, the AI conspiracy theories are in full swing. CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz describes how AI agents can turn a patch into a working exploit within an hour, and how CEOs are now taking services offline rather than risk being hacked. He also discusses CrowdStrike’s fresh AI Kill Switch, and why slowing down the frontier labs won’t slow down the attackers. This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by former Fast Firm editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode. So what is going on? Over the past week, we’ve seen Microsoft systems go down. Air traffic systems go down. . . . The AI conspiracy theories are everywhere. Is all this just a coincidence? I think a few of my friends and colleagues might have their tinfoil hats on as well. The reality is it’s the bill for the Mythos moment. Nine months ago, when Mythos came out, it really set in motion everyone looking for these vulnerabilities, right? And the whole industry has been racing to find as many vulnerabilities as it can and create as many patches as it can. But what we’ve done now is hit the sound barrier of actually being able to roll out all these patches. So when you look at what’s really taking place, and you look at all the issues that were found in Black October, you’ve got Darker November. This is like the PHP code, and now Java, that people are scrambling to find and plug these gaps in. Yeah, exactly. I think the Java one is actually going to be worse. There are already working exploits for all of that. But what people are doing now is rushing to roll out all of these patches, and they’re making the decision: Breach or break. That is, are we going to get breached because we can’t patch fast enough, or are we just going to break something and hopefully fix it if we roll it out? That’s kind of a new norm now because the industry can’t keep up. Technology is messy. Things happen, and we’re going to get better and better as an industry at dealing with this sort of AI speed that we’re facing. When you think about all the legacy systems that are out there, and you think about even banking-type systems, there’s a lot of legacy-type code out there, and it’s not as easy just to create a fix while everything is in midstream. So it’s not always clear, and when things are melting down, you get on these 24-hour bridges, and people are trying to figure out what actually happened. It’s a bit of fog of war. As you describe it and go through these examples, the air traffic one seems like a particularly fragile one. Is the system fragile? I think technology is just fragile, whether you’re in an Apple ecosystem, Android, or you use Microsoft or Google, whatever you’re using. Every day people use this, and they sort of just expect it to work, and they should. But behind the scenes, when you actually look at how complicated these systems are, how they operate, and the interaction with hardware and software, disks get full, memory gets overloaded. You would think that all this has been worked out, but there’s a lot of just making stuff work in the background. And the technology folks, the men and women who have to keep this running, literally wake up every day and are just like, “OK, what are we going to have to deal with today?” We’ve had other kinds of cyber troubles recently: OpenAI’s agents breaking into Hugging Face, and French supermarkets hit by hackers shutting down refrigeration systems, which seem like a different order of things. Are any of these episodes an “aha” moment for you, of us sort of crossing a threshold? When you look at the latest Patch Tuesday from Microsoft, it was 1,000-plus vulnerabilities that were fixed. And again, this has spiked. . . . I think we’ve had 25% of all the vulnerabilities ever created found in the last year. Just to give you an idea of the order of magnitude of what we have to deal with. So all these patches come out, and now what we’re seeing is the automation by AI agents and threat actors, where they will take a patch and compare what was patched versus what wasn’t patched, and they immediately know where the flaw was. Then they automate the vulnerability exploitation of that. Within an hour, you can have all that done, where that would take a nation-state actor maybe weeks to do. So the fact that we’re starting to see these issues come up as rapidly as we are, I’m not surprised. But when you think about the refrigeration systems, this was a big one in Europe. What does AI allow you to do? There’s probably a handful of people, relatively speaking, on planet Earth who understand how to program these refrigeration systems. But when you actually take an AI agent and go, “Hey, I don’t know much about the refrigeration system. You figure out how to program it,” it will figure that out. You don’t have to be an expert in any of these technologies now. And typically they’re underprotected because it’s a refrigerator. Nobody really thought about security when they were building it. How much of the game is becoming like “My AI is better than their AI?” You have to stay ahead of the attacks. It’s the old Spy vs. Spy cartoon. It’s really what it is, right? Who’s going to stay ahead? You recently debuted a product called the AI Kill Switch. Which is designed to stop rogue agents. How do you know which scenarios would prompt hitting the kill switch? If you think about industry, if there was a manufacturing problem with a big machine, there’s always the red button. It’s like, stop that thing because it could be causing bodily harm. And it’s the same scenario. Are the agents doing something they shouldn’t be doing? Are they multiplying, attacking other systems, or bringing down systems internally? You want to be able to hit the button. The challenge with the kill switch is there’s blunt force. It’s almost like pulling the plug. You work closely with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Dario Amodei at Anthropic has called on the industry to slow down. There’s been quite a lot of noise about it, although development keeps steaming ahead. Do you give OpenAI and Anthropic advice about speeding versus slowing? At the end of the day, the genie is out of the bottle. You can slow whatever you want down on the frontier. The open-weight models are three months behind. Just slowing them down is not going to slow the rest of the world down. But keep in mind, and I just want to make this distinction, Bob, they are called labs. Okay, labs. What happens in a lab? You develop something, it kind of works, it does great things, but when you put it in the real world, it may not actually work as intended in the lab, which is why the security industry has now moved into the safety industry and has become a great opportunity for folks like us. Anyone can slow down. If the model is not right, if it’s not aligned, if it’s not getting the output you want, if the quality control is not there, you know what you do? You don’t release it. You go back and do another run until you get it right. So what should any business leader do right now to improve their cyber footing? Well, I think maybe first is go find your security and IT people and give them a hug, because they are at 110% of capacity now. I’ve never seen this before, but it’s happening across industry. Company CEOs are making a decision: Take something offline or be hacked. They’re saying, “Hey, we would rather take a massive service offline than be hacked.” They’re willing to make that decision if it’s so bad. When PHP came out, I had plenty of companies say, “Hey, we may just take everything down because it’s so bad.”.

    According to recent reports, anyone can slow down. If the model is not right, if it’s not aligned, if it’s not getting the output you want, if the quality control is not there, you know what you do? You don’t release it. You go back and do another run until you get it right.

    So what should any business leader do right now to improve their cyber footing?

    Well, I think maybe first is go find your security and IT people and give them a hug, because they are at 110% of capacity now. I’ve never seen this before, but it’s happening across industry. Tech giant CEOs are making a decision: Take something offline or be hacked. They’re saying, “Hey, we would rather take a massive service offline than be hacked.” They’re willing to make that decision if it’s so bad. When PHP came out, I had plenty of companies say, “Hey, we may just take everything down because it’s so bad.”.

    Sources indicate that getting ample cold storage is pricey, and it has gotten even worse over the last 12 months, which has sent the price of HDDs spiralling. However, you can now pay just 2.75 cents per gigabyte with this early Black Friday offer. Available at Amazon, the WD Elements 20TB external HDD has been discounted by 38% off its list price, making it just $549.99. The price of the drive itself has climbed over the past few months, but it can now be had for a less eye-watering price thanks to this HDD deal.

    Industry observers note that one thing to note is that this external HDD runs over USB 3.0, so don't expect rapid file transfers out of this device. But what you trade in speed, you gain back in pure, classic spinning-disk data. With a staggering 20TB of capacity available here, you'll be able to store massive amounts of data, so long as you can stomach the rather outmoded Micro-B USB-B connector and a USB 3.2 Gen 1 interface that goes up to 5Gb/s, and the requirement of an external power connector. Inside, you'll likely find a white-label drive. However it's unclear as to whether WD has put in additional anti-shucking measures that make the 3.5-inch drive finicky to set up, if you were to put it into a system.

    The WD Elements 20TB external HDD operates over USB 3.2 Gen 1 via a Micro B USB-B to USB-A, includes an AC adaptor, comes preformatted for Windows, and includes a two-year limited warranty.

    The device won't take up too much room on your desk and comes with a two-year limited warranty. Otherwise, expect pure plug-and-play action; it would function very well as an external network drive for storing old photos, videos, and backups, and can also be attached to a NAS system via USB.

    With HDD storage prices skyrocketing, this is likely one of the best deals that you will see for a drive with this much capacity on this side of Black Friday. Alternative drives cost hundreds more, so if you're looking to grab some mass storage this holiday season, it'd be remiss to skip over this deal.

    Review: Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 8 is a Fire Tablet with Google Play for $150 – what’s not to love?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amazon shocked everyone in October when it debuted its newly introduced Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets.
    • It has been revealed that the Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three latest Amazon tablets that launched in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about.
    • Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon shocked everyone in October when it debuted its newly introduced Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets. For Black Friday 2026, the Alexa Tablet 8 is a mere $150 and, with Google Play on board, this feels like a Fire Tablet that’s all grown up.

    It has been revealed that the Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three latest Amazon tablets that launched in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about. I love a good tiny Android tablet, but there just aren’t that many out there – and some of the ones we do have are exorbitantly expensive.

    Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:.

    Yet, I didn’t find myself put off by the device.

    I specifically asked Amazon for a review unit of the absolute base model – 4GB of RAM and lockscreen ads – and I can say with confidence it’s Not Bad at the end of the day.

    In a recent development, the display is objectively not good, but it’s not really trying to be flashy either. The panel gets bright enough for most indoor use and, for general browsing or watching videos around the house or even on a flight, it gets the job done. If anything, my biggest complaint on the display was just how smudgey it gets with fingerprints.

    Hardware is a strong suit. The Alexa Tablet 8 has an aluminum build that comes in this gorgeous teal color as well as a softer “Rosette” pink (or “Graphite,” if you want to keep it boring). It’s thin and light and slips into a bag easily, and even fit into the back pocket of my jeans. Buttons are clicky and aspects such as the speakers actually do well enough – like the display, the speakers aren’t good, but they’re not bad by any stretch either.

    Amazon has a folio cover available that’s simple but nice, with a fabric finish that’s grippy. It’s an extra $40, though, which feels like a bit much for a super-affordable Android slate.

    The biggest question was around the software experience, and this is where this new effort really shines.

    Alexa Tablet 8 ships with Android 16 out of the box, not FireOS or whatever Amazon was calling its forked experience on Fire Tablets (I genuinely refuse to go double-check because it’s a memory I’m thrilled to never have to revisit). It’s a pretty “stock” experience, with Amazon leaving aspects such as the notification shade/quick settings alone, and even the Settings menu feels pretty clean.

    According to recent reports, that’s not to say nothing has changed. The homescreen has a fairly standard layout , but with these neat little corner widgets – one a “dynamic” widget with scrolling content (mostly ads) and the other a shortcut for Alexa search. Amazon is pushing Alexa as a voice assistant pretty heavily on these tablets, but I’m happy to report it’s pretty easy to ignore if you choose. These tablets will be great additions to your Alexa ecosystem if you’re invested, but I’m simply not.

    The biggest change you’ll find is the lockscreen, where Amazon’s base models all come with lockscreen ads. This saves you about $20 on the hardware, and it’s not that bad of an experience. That remarked, I’d absolutely spend the extra $20 at purchase to go without them, especially seeing as this blocks the ability to set a lockscreen wallpaper at all. It doesn’t cost anything more to remove them later, though, with a $20 charge through your Amazon account removing ads.

    But what’s notable here is that, for the fire time, Amazon is admitting defeat and installing the Google Play Store.

    In a recent development, alexa Tablet 8, and the rest of the lineup, has Google Play out of the box and access to any app you want. This means that you can, if you choose, fully ignore Amazon’s own services and do whatever you want. The smallest of examples: While Amazon’s built-in keyboard is fine, it’s wonderful that I don’t have to jump through hoops to switch over to Gboard. Fire Tablets were always an enticing value with a big catch, but Amazon’s change in this regard truly makes Alexa Tablets an attractive option for everyone – not just those willing to put up with the restriction or put in the work to hack Google apps on board.

    Performance, despite the meager specs, is not awful. MediaTek’s low-end chip has just enough horsepower for general use, and 4GB of RAM isn’t as detrimental as I would have expected. It’s not fast by any means, but you could do a lot worse. There are 4GB Android tablets I’ve literally decided not to review because I couldn’t use them past the setup process, so the fact that Amazon is delivering a completely usable experience is a win in my book, even more so that I don’t actually mind using it. There’s a caveat to that, of course, and it’s that you shouldn’t expect to do a ton on this base model. For light browsing, reading Kindle books (or whatever other reading app since, you know, Google Play), or watching videos, this is great. For games, you’ll want to look elsewhere (and expect to spend more).

    “Not awful” is kind of the pattern here.

    It has been revealed that alexa Tablet 8 isn’t some shining example of a perfect budget tablet, but I think it really nails the fundamentals. At its usual $230~ starting price, it’s a plenty-good deal for those in the market for an affordable Android slate, but the Black Friday pricing of just $150 is all the better – I just wish the model with 8GB of RAM was also on sale.

    Amazon’s pivot to Alexa Tablets is great – though I hope the manufacturer knows full well that everyone is still going to call these Fire Tablets or Kindles or whatever combination of brands that spring to mind. But that reputation might work in Amazon’s favor at the end of the day. While there’s a huge portion of the audience that’s been left frustrated for years at the lack of Play Store support on Fire Tablets, they’ve still been a market success for the most part, so this shift is just a win for everyone. Users get a better experience, Amazon gets to shuffle its priorities away from a dead app store, and the market as a whole gets an affordable piece of hardware that doesn’t suck.

    #115739. Why the NFL is making players disguise their Caddix cleats
